entry.title: Vibe Coding or Rubber Ducking? I Think The Latter

link.title: Vibe Coding or Rubber Ducking? I Think The Latter

entry.content:
I have a grudge to share. When people in Jeeps started claiming the rubber ducks, I was upset. Now ‘vibe coding’ is doing the same! But I know what you are thinking—‘What is this ducking guy talking about?’.

Rubber Ducking

I’ll start by explaining Rubber Ducking—and no, get your mind out of the gutter, don’t even know what you might have thought.

For me, and I think a lot of Computer Science friends, Rubber Ducking was an initiation ceremony. Usually—as it happened to me—in the first programming class, the teacher would enter the classroom with a bag filled with rubber ducks: One for each class mate. It would be explained that this was our troubleshooting buddy.

When debugging, planning, or writing an algorithm, there is always a time we hit a wall. Like the old philosopher said, the answer lies within thyself. But how do we unlock it?

The mind is layered; if we give equal importance to all the information we have to compute, anxiety would kick in. Most of the control we think we have over our thoughts, we do not—hence hypnotists, magicians, psychiatrists, etc…

The duck is just a tool to guide our minds to a focus state. I’m overdramatizing a lot of the explanation; we were never told anything beyond; “talk to it and ask a question you may find yourself answering the question”.

I think this is true. Explaining things to someone—or something—helps us realize what we thought we understood, and what we actually do. When we verbalize or write something we use inference just as LLMs (Large Language Models) do; we may find by induction, deduction or abduction what we are missing. Or simply be honest and say I don’t know or don’t have enough information.

We can do that in our heads, but we all know some things sound much better in our minds than when they come out. So, that’s Rubber Ducking: your faithful troubleshooting buddy. Too bad it doesn’t talk back—wait a minute!!

Agentic LLMs (Large Language Models) CLI (Command Line Interface)

The duck can now talk back! The first experience for most people would be your Chat GPT or Gemini console on a browser. These are fine and can give you the answers you are looking for but generally they are used more as an enhanced search.

These CLIs are different, programmers are more comfortable with them; they can be opened into a secluded project directory; and they have tools. Yes tools! They can write, delete or modify files.

I’ll explain my own experience with it. For example this Blog project is AI assisted, big word ASSISTED. For example when trying to figure out how to use jakyll; or how to run it locally to test; even how to organize my directory structure for better viewing.

Vibe Coding

Vibe Coding, what is that? One way I think of it is musically. I guess I could say I’ve done Vibe Composing before. When young I used to spend nights hooped on coffee until 3, 4 in the morning sometimes even seeing the sunrise. I usually keep a recording of what I’ve done, and always went to bed—during the day—excited about it. Plenty of times when sober (off the coffee) I listen to it and cringed, who wrote this blasphemy? Me. A lot of times there were ideas to be salvaged and may even have yielded something that could be good.

Vibe Coding is pretty much it. You have tools doing the work for you. You use natural language to tell the LLM what you need and the LLM spits out a chunk of code that is supposed to do what you told it to do. All and all that’s fine, except that LLMs aren’t perfect and even when spot on it may give you what you asked and not what you really need. We don’t always know what we want and the answer comes through trials and iterations. So vibing is like the LLM hooped on coffee, spitting out sometimes clunky chunky code that does what you asked but may not smell great, yeah code smells, that’s a thing.

When the code doesn’t smell right we have to trouble shoot. We often want to modify, optimize, prettify, enhance what we thought we wanted. When LLMs write clunky chunky code it’s hard to follow and oftentimes you’d be stepping on the LLM’s toes when modifying things. I know it first hand. I modify some code then ask the LLM to implement something else and then the LLM just deletes everything I do.

LLMs as Your Rubber Duck

I think it is safe to say that building things on sections will guarantee you best maintainability and coherence. Well, coherence and coupling are different topics, but even when prototyping with a tightly coupled idea we probably still want some separation. Separating your ideas into parts will help you use the LLM as a Rubber Duck, not write a bulky app to do this one thing, but collaborate with it to write different parts of what you need. This way you discover what you need and end up building something much better than you first imagined.

Using LLMs as a Rubber Duck stands apart from Vibing. Now we are talking about Assisted Coding which I think is a much better term then Vibing. Now we can leverage agents to do different parts of a project and not completely lose control. It’s a difficult balance between high level awareness and low level understanding. As programmers, we usually leave high level awareness to middle management and focus on the low level understanding to do our jobs. Sometimes, especially if working on a personal project, we have to be both. Using LLMs as Assisted Coding tools will yield much better results than the Vibe idea of just build me this.

Cautionary Tale

Using an LLM to assist you requires that you work as equals. Always question the LLM suggestions and implementations. I remember troubleshooting a problem at work where we were subindexing with decimals, as in 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2, … So this part of the code rarely sees subindexes greater than x.9, so the order was always right. Well it happened that although rare it does occur and things were out of order because 1.2 is greater than 1.10. Well out of curiosity I asked Gemini about whether 1.2 is greater than 1.10. It said it was wrong. I then ask to look it up to confirm it. It said it couldn’t do that because 1.10 is greater than 1.2 and it wouldn’t waste its time looking it up, not exactly what it said just paraphrasing it. I had to look up myself to keep my sanity and I insisted that it did an internet search on it. This time it did and it confirmed the correct answer 1.2 is greater than 1.10, admitting it was wrong in the most minimal way possible.

So the problem is not just that LLMs will make mistakes but that it will make believable mistakes. It will stick by it. It will give a very good explanation to why it is right. In the end I spent my ride home questioning myself whether 1.10 was greater than 1.2 just because of how confident the LLM was. If we don’t keep things small and make sure we supervise every change mistakes will creep up. Once the amount of code is reasonably hard it becomes a nightmare to find where the little broken parts are.

entry.title: Pipeline Efficiency X Goal Completion Part III

link.title: Pipeline Efficiency X Goal Completion Part III

entry.content:
Back on this again, but I swear this should only take 300 words. Well maybe, max 500, or 550-ish. To recap, we discussed ways to automate and optimize. When we engage in these activities, we spend a lot of time planning and visualizing. This is the time we don’t spend on completing tasks.

The book, Software Engineering at Google, has some great topics. The most memorable, and I paraphrase: some things are important but not urgent and some things are urgent but not important. A good engineer is one that knows when to drop the ball. How I see this is: {there is always going to be something urgent to do. Urgent things are menial, they are short-lived, and are usually something imposed on you by others. The important things are usually not urgent because they have a long project horizon or a protracted completion so we keep postponing them, out of procrastination or someone else’s will imposed on you—yeah, money, the boss, the government, your mom or something}.

When you have something important in life that involves one task or many tasks, these always have to do with change. We want to activate or instill change in ourselves, in others, in our environment.

Creating pipelines or automating how we do things are structural in nature. These will give us the best long-term benefits because change needs to be structural; otherwise it will be superficial and eventually irrelevant. Meaningful change comes from behavioral change, whether good or bad.

A lot of people like the illusion of talent.

Yeah, fish are very good at swimming, birds can fly, and monkeys climb trees. Everyone is different and is fighting their own battles. But us humans tend to attribute incredible achievement with a godly given gift from Jesus, Buddha, Titans, Orixas—pick your poison. Nobody is looking for the kid or adult (never late to start anything) who spends 8, or 2, or 1 hour a day playing guitar; or reading math books and academic papers; or coding and reading tech docs; or playing soccer; or painting… for years and years to come, never-ending.

How do they do it? if I answered here, you would think I’m accomplished [laughs at self], so I won’t do that. But what I would say is: I think that the reason some people can keep up the work, and get really good, is not perfection. They make mistakes, they weren’t that great at some point, they may even have sucked. But they enjoyed what they did and continued. They developed algorithms that governed their lives. That allowed them to continue, and when they failed, they could get back up because they had a method.

Only change in behavior has long-lasting effects. It is the most difficult change, but it is the one that will guarantee you success. Not because of some magic potion that will make your dreams come true, but because of stubborn, relentless repetition. In martial arts or artistic fields, people say—you have to do something ten thousand times to become an expert. Anyone that has done something ten thousand times is not just doing something; organic methods or structures are built out of the effort. I bet if you spend more time working the process/pipeline than in just grinding the tasks, you could probably do it in five thousand repetitions and who knows maybe less.

entry.title: Pipeline Efficiency X Goal Completion Part II

link.title: Pipeline Efficiency X Goal Completion Part II

entry.content:
Pipeline Efficiency X Goal Completion Part II

Making a decision on whether to spend time automating a set of tasks or checking off the tasks one-by-one is difficult. If you “just do it” (Not sponsored by Nike), you can get them out of the way quickly. If you choose to take the time and optimize the process, it will be sluggish, and you might not even get to any of the tasks right away. But which is best? Sounds like an easy answer.

Most people just do it, and yes, this may be the best way sometimes, but then when should automation and optimization be taken into account?

To me a good rule of thumb is frequency. Once you realize that task/s is/are done frequently we can check complexity: how many tasks is this workflow composed of? Lastly but maybe closely related to frequency is the project horizon— how long is the project? Some might be life long projects others; one-and-done and are so infrequent you may not want to worry about.

This Blog for example started as just a small practice exercise on writing. As a musician, I can guarantee you that a skill you don’t practice is a skill you will gradually lose.

So the frequency is meant to be sporadic with a vanishing horizon and a healthy size workflow that grows as I learn. When I started, the idea was to also explore a few technological tools, and frameworks. I already talked about github as a host and jekyll as an engine in a different blog. These technologies do a lot of work in the background to serve what you are reading. In the Software Engineering world we call this abstraction.

We abstract away the things that are fundamental—sometimes through inheritance—and things that are parallel because we want to focus on the task at hand. We encapsulate these parallel parts so we safeguard all processes by ensuring rules and controlling accessibility. We also encourage reusability by abstracting: this way, we build the wheel only once. We can promote polymorphism to reduce duplication, and extend or override if necessary—this is off-topic here; I think I wrote quite a bit about OOP (Object Oriented Programming) in my undergrad years.

So, choosing and using a framework is a first form of pipelining, or maybe choosing the pipes. One of the first technologies I wanted to try was using LLM CLI (Large Language Model; Command Line Interface) as a project assistant. I wanted to try that after watching this YouTube video. If you are into tech, you should watch it. It is a whole topic, and I won’t get into it here. In a nutshell, it can read and write files in a folder or project and is extremely helpful—sometimes not. I will probably write about my experience using LLMs separately. To do this I had to read some documentation, and set a few things up, DevOps.

Choice of operating systems matters and Windows is not the most helpful. Thankfully I had WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) installed. This shows how things we learn or do and set up in the past have a surprising way of becoming helpful in the future, which are unforeseen—Oposite of Tech-Debt Tech-Credit, I guess more like Tech-Savings or investment: pick your analogy.

While working through this project, I started to see a few things I was doing, which would become repetitive in the future. Nothing wrong with repetitive; we want things to be standardized, so work is predictable. And if it is predictable, it can be automated; the more you automate, the greater flexibility you have with the creative parts that can’t and shouldn’t be automated.

I started with the Social Media Card. I’ll be open to you here: I don’t claim to know about Social-Engineering—(insert laugh emoji here) that’s more like DevSec—just a play on words, this should be more like Social-Media-Engineering. [A million dollar idea, tech consultancy for influencers: you can use it, I’ll only take 3%.]

So, since I’m not too savvy on web development, this is also a learning experience. A Social Media Card is something that is embedded in the HTML. Social Networks use this to render how you see something when you share a link. The meta tags are standard, and anyone can add them.

Jekyll engine would create these meta tags automatically when the config part of the blog has the address for the image to be used. I didn’t want just the background image to be used, so I decided to use the abstract/excerpt to display some portion of the text. Doing this over and over again is time-consuming. That’s not what this project was about. I would have to do it for every blog—so maybe a lot, or maybe not.

I decided to automate that. Using Python and a few image-editing libraries I created a program to resize the background image, find the excerpt and write on the image, and save it as a separate image just for the media card in the appropriate folder.

When I tried it out, I realized that the font looked wonky, because a small number of words needed a bigger font, and a large number of words should have a smaller font. I automated the size of the font by word count using five discrete sizes per some defined word count. I learned a few things and now this frees up time because when I’m ready I just run the script and a social card is built for me.

I apologize if this text is too long. I’ve been trying to be less technical because at work I’ve been told that I am too technical talking to specialists. Then my brother reads this and tells me I am not technical enough. I am trying to do both, but being a little extra technical means things get a little long winded. In this case about 1000 words.

We’ll need Part III for this blog but I promise this should be the last time. I’ll put a cap on the word count as well.

entry.title: Pipeline Efficiency X Goal Completion Part I

link.title: Pipeline Efficiency X Goal Completion Part I

entry.content:
Pipeline Efficiency X Goal Completion

We all come to a time in life when we realize we have too many projects or tasks to complete. This could be as simple as mowing the lawn, putting out the laundry, or paying the bills, or as complex as building an app, writing a song, or learning a new technology. (Staying away from long term goals here like getting a degree/certificate or a new career.)

Goals permeate our lives. Big or small, we spend most of our days performing tasks. Sometimes a goal involves only one task and can be completed in a single pass. Other goals can be composed of many tasks and may even take multiple passes. One thing every goal has in common is time. Accomplishing things takes time, and saving time on accomplishing things allows us to do more because we have more time.

In tech we use the term pipeline as the process to move code to a repository. Pipelines can be complex and do many things, such as validation, integration, consolidation—it really has to do with automation. This delves into DevOps, a very complex topic. I have a lot of respect for people in that field. If we didn’t have this type of work, things would be much harder.

I want to mention pipelines here more as a workflow. I would even use the literal reference of being a plumber. Pipes live in the background; no one ever looks at them, but you know when they are not working well or break. A plumber could also look at a bad plumber’s work and know all the inefficiencies that can turn into problems or slow the flow.

Another term we use in tech that applies to this is tech-debt. We could also call it life-debt and mirror it. An example would be: you work and pay your mortgage but never call a plumber to do preventive maintenance. All of the sudden, things break or slow down—as they should when not maintained.

So, I’ll move away from the proper term definition of pipeline here. My idea of pipeline here is to move things from an incomplete state to complete. Many people, for example, when putting away their laundry, do it the brute force way—from the machine to the hangers. Others throw it in bed and separate them into sections before putting it away (me). The moral of the story here is there are many ways to do the same thing. Some are more efficient; some not so much.

We usually like to spend time on things that offer immediate or quick rewards. This sometimes equates to doing the tasks and not taking the time to make them easier to do in the future. Working on the pipeline or algorithm takes time, and most of the time it will deny you the immediate or quick reward of a task done. After all, LifeOps like DevOps are difficult tasks that need to be done as well.

entry.title: A Search Epiphany
entry.content:
A Search Epiphany

Last week I worked on a project to relearn some classical guitar songs I knew. I reached a song I needed to revisit, and thankfully, I had a video recording of me playing it. The video was about 10 years old. I had no sheet music, and I named the title misleadingly. This led me down the path of the search, the failure, and the epiphany of a method to re-search when stuck. I guess I should start with a quick run down of where I was this week.

The Need For a Search

This project, as I stated, is to relearn most of the songs I used to know for Classical guitar (Maybe a subject for its own blog). This week I reached seven relearned songs, and today, 11/09/25, I have begun the process of learning eight. All I had was the video of me playing on my youtube channel- A mess, I won’t even share here; maybe someday I’ll clean it up. The first thing I usually do is look up for a free PDF of the song score by name. Easy, right? Not quite. When I searched, I realized that I probably didn’t know the name of the song then and put the wrong one in the title.

The First Failure

Realizing that the title was wrong, I began a simple search. Such as, “what songs are similar to this Bach song for guitar?”. At least I had somewhere to start. I knew the author. But think about it: How many songs Bach wrote? I’ll let you do a search on that. Didn’t really get too far on it. My better guess was, let’s start on plan B.

Plan B, Even If You Don’t Have One Make One Up

Plan B is simple: I have the video and a good pair of ears. I grew up in an age where I had to pick up songs by ear, and I didn’t have a whole lot of tools or tutorials to help. I usually do a half-and-half approach even if I find the score or sheet music. The reason is that sometimes I play things in my own way…

Alright, this is off-topic. Let’s go back.

Learning by ear is hard, especially for Bach. He does everything in counterpoint with melodies that move in different directions, each with its own behavior. If music were visual, to see everything that was done, you would need chameleon eyes that move independently. Never mind that—for some instances, you’d need the visual degree of freedom of a chameleon’s eye plus spider or bee multiple vision subdivision.

Plan A is Faster Try it Again

So, while I was at the gym, I was frustrated with my last attempt. I actually learned the first five seconds with Plan B, and while doing that, I discovered that I was playing in a different guitar tuning, which made this just so much harder. I started to think (someday I should write about how I use the gym to exercise thinking and let my brain go wild), “How can I solve this problem?” Plan A is just that much better. The reference is there—I can forget it and always get back to it. I can read it in smaller chunks. I don’t know; being able to read and write music is something I should be exercising as much as I can anyway.

Epiphany

So I used Shazam to do it! Good idea, right? Not so much, I say. It found a Techno song, and some other weird stuff unrelated and finally said, Sorry can’t find it. All I needed was a name but all I had was a video I made—with the wrong title. I went up to different machines and listened to Tech podcasts; and reading coding framework docs; and something came to my mind. Wait a minute, my search is too broad. I have to nest this, remove its degrees of freedom. So my next search was—give me a list of Bach songs that are arranged for Classical Guitar; sort the list by popularity. It gave me a List of 10 songs, I then asked. Give me links to video rendition of these songs. While listening to these songs I found what I needed.

Lesson of The Day

Sometimes we need something that is specific. We know exactly what we need, but we can’t really find it. Tools need some fine-tuning to give you a smaller sample of what to look for. Even with a smaller sample, some things cannot be done by smart machines. You have to walk some of the way on your own.

You can use stochastic methods to get deterministic results, like the name of a song. In the end, I was able to say which one was the right one. A brute-force approach is never best. Sometimes, a collage of methods is what is needed.

Creating a list of songs was brute-force; ordering by popularity, stochastic; listening to the first 10 to find the right one, deterministic. So, the best approach may be a mix of different approaches.

entry.title: Introduction
entry.content:
Introduction

Hi, nice to see you are catching this excerpt. I have decided on improving my writing and polishing my knowledge through this blog as a writing exercise. You should expect topics on music, technology, and miscellaneous non-confrontational topics. This should be no longer than 500 words, and to tell the truth, I may just stick to 300 words for the most part. Since this is a living experiment, the formats may change, but for the most part, I want to keep this light and informative.

As a first topic, I believe talking about how this blog was built should be a priority. This first blog is just a placeholder so I can research and learn how to use GitHub Pages for this. Maybe this is a good place to talk about the experience. To tell the truth, I think maintaining a blog like this is doable if you don’t have a tech background, but it is possible that you can get caught in the process and give up. My job here will be to try to create a boilerplate (sample code) so that someone can start from a built, simple framework.

I have many friends who don’t have a lot of experience with GitHub repositories or any other repository, as a matter of fact, so I’ll just explain what it is here quickly. GitHub (Microsoft) or GitLab (Google has a stake) are just repositories for information. For the most part, it is used for code, but a lot of people use it for different things such as blogs, short stories, books, DIY projects—really all kinds of things. This is a good video to watch to start on GitHub; you can also, if you are not a video person, read this documentation. I myself, if I didn’t have a tech background, would skim through the documentation and take a quick look at the video. To tell you the truth, I think the documentation is enough.

Why GitHub/GitLab? A lot of people use it, and it is a platform where you can not only share your ideas but also collaborate with others or share your projects for others to collaborate. To prove that, I’ll give you here my vanilla version of this blog. I will call it the Vanilla Blog. I will show you how to fork it and start your own blog if you feel like it.

Once you have your own GitHub account, you can sign in. Afterward, you can follow the provided link. You could also just go straight to the link; it might prompt you to sign in there. On the right side of your screen, you’ll see three buttons: Watch, Fork, and Star. Give it a Star if you like, but really, just click on the Fork button (it may be a drop-down) and select Create Fork. You’ll be sent to a page where you can rename the project.

It will bring you to your copy of the project page. You don’t have a live web page yet; you need to set it up. Go to the Settings tab. On the left side, under the Code and Automation section, choose Pages. Keep Deploy from branch, and for the Branch, select main (or master) instead of None. Click Save. You can go to the Actions tab to see the build process. Once the build is done, go back to the Code tab. On the right side of the screen, if you scroll down, you will see Deployments. Click on the latest one; it will take you to a page with the link. Click on the link, and it will bring you to your live page.

The blog itself should show you how to edit and create new posts. If you are stuck or unsure, always remember: you are one step away from the answer if you can use a search engine and read documentation. Happy blogging! I hope this can be of help for some. It certainly was for me to set this up and learn a few things in the process.

Good bye!
